subskill: form: subject-verb agreement with a foreign plural subject and tense set by a habitual clause
passage: Stream ecologists count caddisfly larvae to gauge water quality, because caddisflies tolerate very little pollution. The larvae ______ beneath a flat stone on the streambed whenever the water temperature drops below about four degrees Celsius. A survey taken during a cold snap can therefore badly undercount a healthy population, and field guides advise sampling on milder days.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject is "larvae," the plural of "larva"; its -ae ending can look singular, but it names many insects, so the verb must be plural. The habitual clause later in the same sentence, "whenever the water temperature drops," uses the present tense, so the main verb must also be present: "are motionless." "is motionless" has the right tense but treats "larvae" as singular. "were motionless" is plural but past, which cannot pair with the present-tense "whenever ... drops." "was motionless" is wrong in both number and tense.
topic_tag: freshwater entomology: caddisfly larvae in cold water

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement after a postposed adjective phrase and pronoun reference to an agent in a preceding clause
passage: Mixed meadows attract the field vole; pastures thick with a single coarse grass ______ almost entirely, because such a uniform sward offers poor cover and little food. Small-mammal surveys on dairy farms find the same contrast again and again. Farmers who want to keep voles away from stored hay sometimes sow that grass along field margins for exactly this reason.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject of the second clause is "pastures"; "thick with a single coarse grass" only describes them, so the singular "grass" does not set the verb's number, and the verb must be the plural "are avoided." The pronoun names whatever avoids the pastures, and the only possible agent in the sentence is "the field vole" in the first clause, which is singular and takes "it"; the sentence's plural "meadows" cannot avoid a pasture. "is avoided by it" has the right pronoun but makes the verb agree with "grass." "are avoided by them" has the right verb but a pronoun with no possible referent, and "is avoided by them" is wrong on both counts.
topic_tag: rodent ecology: field voles in grazed pastures

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement with a compound of-object and tense set by a conditional clause
passage: Persistent heartburn can signal damage to tissue that causes no pain at all. The lining of the esophagus and stomach ______ with a thin flexible camera if the burning returns despite a month of medication. A small biopsy of any reddened patch can then show whether the surface cells have begun to change.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject is "lining"; "of the esophagus and stomach" only says which lining, so the compound "esophagus and stomach" does not make the subject plural, and the verb must be singular. The conditional clause in the same sentence, "if the burning returns," is in the present tense, so the main verb must also be present: "is examined." "are examined" has the right tense but agrees with the compound. "was examined" is singular but past, which cannot pair with "if the burning returns," and "were examined" is wrong in both number and tense.
topic_tag: gastroenterology: endoscopy for persistent heartburn

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement with a distributive subject and verb aspect set by a definite-past time phrase
passage: Harvest after harvest ______ on the steep, eroded terraces of one mountain valley some sixty years ago. Agronomists who study soil loss often cite the valley as a warning. Local farmers blame the poor yields on the collapse of the dry-stone walls that held the soil in place, and agronomists agree that the walls mattered more than any choice of crop.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: A subject of the form "harvest after harvest" names one harvest at a time and takes a singular verb, even though the repetition suggests many. The phrase "some sixty years ago," at the end of the same sentence, places the situation at a finished point in the past, so the simple past is needed: "was meager." "has been meager" is singular, but the present perfect cannot combine with a definite past time such as "sixty years ago." "were meager" is past but plural, and "have been meager" is wrong in both number and form.
topic_tag: soil conservation: collapsed terrace walls

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement with a compound subject and possessive pronoun reference to the compound
passage: A typical apple tree sold by a commercial nursery is really two plants, joined at a graft just above the soil line. The fruiting scion and its dwarfing rootstock ______ genes, and no DNA passes across the union. Seeds from the fruit therefore inherit nothing from the rootstock, not even the compact size that growers prize.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject is the compound "the fruiting scion and its dwarfing rootstock": two plants joined by "and," so the verb must be plural, "have." The possessive names the owner of the genes, and the text says the two plants are separate and that "no DNA passes across the union," so each part owns its genes and the plural "their" is needed. "has its own" and "has their own" treat the subject as the single noun "rootstock" before the blank. "have its own" has a plural verb but a singular possessive that cannot refer to the two-part subject.
topic_tag: pomology: apple scions and dwarfing rootstocks

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement and auxiliary choice in verb-phrase ellipsis
passage: A survey of soybean growers in one farming region confirms a familiar rule of weed control: resistance spreads fastest on farms that rely on a single herbicide and never rotate to another. Weeds resistant to glyphosate have appeared in fields across the region, and a resistant form of giant ragweed ______ too.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The blank stands for a shortened verb phrase that repeats the first clause's verb, "have appeared," so it needs the same auxiliary, a form of "have." Its subject is "a resistant form of giant ragweed," whose head "form" is singular; the plural "Weeds" belongs to the first clause. So the correct choice is "has." "have" copies the first clause's auxiliary but also its plural number. "does" and "do" would stand for a simple-present verb such as "appears," not for "have appeared," and "do" is plural as well.
topic_tag: weed management: glyphosate-resistant ragweed

subskill: boundaries: ending a declarative sentence that contains an indirect question
passage: When a power cut shut down a hospital pharmacy overnight, its staff had to decide which medicines could still be used. The pharmacists needed to know whether the stored vaccines had warmed past eight degrees ______ answer came from small color-changing labels on the vials, which darken permanently above that temperature, so the check took only minutes.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: "The pharmacists needed to know whether the stored vaccines had warmed past eight degrees Celsius" is a complete statement: the question about the vaccines is reported indirectly in a "whether" clause, so the sentence ends with a period, and "Their answer came from ..." begins a new sentence. "Celsius? Their" ends a statement with a question mark, which belongs only to a direct question. "Celsius, their" joins two independent clauses with only a comma, and "Celsius their" joins them with no punctuation at all.
topic_tag: pharmacy practice: vaccine cold-chain checks

subskill: boundaries: attaching a sentence-final participial phrase that describes the subject
passage: Gardeners who pull up a wilting carrot often find the work of the carrot rust fly. The fly's pale larva tunnels just under the skin of the ______ a network of rust-colored channels that soon begin to rot. Damaged carrots cannot be sold, and a single generation of the pest can ruin whole rows.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The sentence is a complete clause, "The fly's pale larva tunnels just under the skin of the root," followed by the participial phrase "leaving a network of rust-colored channels," which describes what the larva does, so a comma sets the phrase off from the clause. "root leaving" attaches the phrase directly to "root," as if the root were leaving the channels. "root: leaving" uses a colon, which must introduce something that explains or lists what the clause names, not a description of the subject's action. "root. Leaving" turns the participial phrase into a sentence fragment with no subject or main verb.
topic_tag: vegetable pests: carrot rust fly larvae

subskill: form: auxiliary choice and subject-verb agreement in verb-phrase ellipsis after a kind-of subject
passage: Sandstone was the cheaper building material in many old towns, and its crumbling surfaces are a common sight on their older streets. Conservators repairing those facades test replacement blocks by soaking and freezing them over and over. Basalt resists the pressure of the expanding ice in such trials, whereas several kinds of quarried sandstone ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject of the whereas-clause is "several kinds of quarried sandstone," whose head "kinds" is plural; "sandstone" sits right before the blank but only names what the kinds are kinds of. The clause ends in verb-phrase ellipsis, so its auxiliary must stand in for the main clause's lexical verb "resists" ("do not [resist the pressure]"), which calls for a form of "do." "does not" uses the right auxiliary but is singular. "are not" is plural but a form of "be" cannot stand in for "resists," and "is not" fails on both counts.
topic_tag: building stone: freeze-thaw durability of facade blocks

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement past a parenthetical list, with tense set by a simultaneous as-clause
passage: A wind-energy laboratory tests full-scale turbine parts before they go to sea. The prototype rotor (a steel hub, a drive shaft, and three fiberglass blades) ______ in strong artificial crosswinds as two engineers watch the strain readings on a monitor. Any blade that flexes beyond its design limit is sent back to the factory for redesign.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject is "The prototype rotor," which is singular; the parentheses only list its parts, so the plural "blades" closing the list does not set the verb's number. The testing happens at the same time as the action in "as two engineers watch," whose verb is present tense, so the verb must be present as well. "are being tested" is present but plural, "was being tested" is singular but past and clashes with "watch," and "were being tested" fails on both counts.
topic_tag: wind engineering: rotor crosswind testing

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement with a deverbal head and two of/by phrases, with tense set by an unless-clause
passage: Radar satellites can detect the swelling of a volcano to within a few millimeters, an early sign that magma is collecting below. The measurements of the summit by both satellites ______ its uplift unless the delay caused by water vapor in the air is removed from the signal. Moist air slows the radar pulses and distorts the apparent height of the ground.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The head of the subject is "measurements," which is plural; "the summit" names what is measured and does not set the number. The sentence is a first conditional: its condition, "unless the delay ... is removed," is in the present tense, so the main verb must be present too. "is overstating" is present but singular, "were overstating" is plural but past and cannot pair with the present "is removed," and "was overstating" fails on both counts.
topic_tag: volcano geodesy: satellite radar uplift

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement with a plural sample noun and a singular of-phrase, with tense set by an until-clause
passage: Polar ice holds tiny bubbles of ancient air, and drilling teams pull it up in long cylinders called cores. Samples of the deepest core ______ in insulated canisters until a supply ship reached the drilling camp at the end of the season. Laboratories that receive such cores compare the trapped air with the modern atmosphere.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The head of the subject is "Samples," which is plural; "the deepest core" right before the blank only says what the samples were taken from. The sealing lasted "until a supply ship reached the drilling camp," and that past-tense verb requires a past-tense main verb. "was sealed" is past but singular, "are sealed" is plural but present and cannot run until a past event, and "is sealed" fails on both counts.
topic_tag: paleoclimatology: deep ice core storage

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement and object pronoun number with the antecedent in an opening place clause
passage: Strain sensors bolted to long-span bridges corrode in a few months if salt and wind reach them, and corroded units report false readings. Engineers who monitor these bridges therefore protect the most exposed instruments first. Wherever the sensors sit on the seaward girders, a thin steel housing ______ from the gusts and the salt spray.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject of the main clause is "a thin steel housing," which is singular, so the verb is "shields"; the plural "sensors" belongs to the opening clause "Wherever the sensors sit on the seaward girders" and is not the subject. The object pronoun must refer back to those plural "sensors," the only things the housing can protect, so it must be "them"; "it" has no possible referent, since the only singular noun before it is the housing itself. "shield them" has the right pronoun but a plural verb, "shields it" has the right verb but a pronoun with nothing to refer to, and "shield it" fails on both counts.
topic_tag: structural health monitoring: bridge strain sensors

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement past a locative phrase, with the auxiliary set by a distant intransitive participle
passage: The tallest dune beside the dry lake beds ______ not, as the early surveys assumed, migrated with the prevailing wind. Soundings of its interior show a core of hard clay anchored to a buried ridge of rock. Geologists who compared aerial photographs from different years had mistaken its shifting crest for movement of the whole dune.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject is "The tallest dune," which is singular; "beside the dry lake beds" only locates it, so the plural "beds" right before the blank does not set the verb's number. After the comment "as the early surveys assumed," the verb continues with "migrated," a past participle of a verb that cannot be passive, so the auxiliary must be a form of "have" ("has not ... migrated"). "have" is the right auxiliary but plural, "was" is singular but would make "was not ... migrated," which is ungrammatical, and "were" fails on both counts.
topic_tag: aeolian geomorphology: dune migration

subskill: boundaries: punctuation between two independent clauses when the second opens with a time phrase
passage: Volcanologists revisit old craters to learn how quickly life returns to bare rock. The lava lake in one summit crater cooled into a hard black ______ a decade ferns had rooted in the cracks of its surface. Mosses and low shrubs followed the ferns, and the crater floor is green today.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: "The lava lake in one summit crater cooled into a hard black crust" is an independent clause, and "within a decade ferns had rooted in the cracks of its surface" is a second independent clause describing a later event. A semicolon correctly joins the two. With a comma alone, the sentence is a comma splice, even though "within a decade" seems at first to belong to "cooled"; with no mark, it is a run-on. A colon would present the second clause as an explanation or elaboration of the first, but the ferns' arrival a decade later neither explains nor restates the cooling.
topic_tag: volcanic ecology: plant colonization of a lava lake

subskill: boundaries: punctuation in a compound predicate joined by and
passage: Old steam boilers develop fatigue cracks where their steel plates are riveted together. A certified welder ground out the cracks along the boiler ______ refilled the grooves with fresh weld metal in thin layers. The welder hammered each layer lightly to relieve stress in the metal before laying down the next.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The sentence has one subject, "A certified welder," and two verbs joined by "and": "ground out the cracks along the boiler seam" and "refilled the grooves." Because "refilled" has no subject of its own, the words after "and" are not an independent clause, and no punctuation belongs between the two parts of the compound predicate. A comma before "and" would wrongly separate the two verbs as though each had its own subject, and a comma after "and" splits the conjunction from the verb it joins. A period would leave "And refilled the grooves with fresh weld metal in thin layers" as a fragment with no subject.
topic_tag: boiler repair: fatigue cracks along riveted seams

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement with a singular indefinite pronoun subject followed by a prepositional phrase ending on a plural noun, crossed with present versus past tense decided by a past-tense verb in a habitual if-clause of the same sentence
passage: Guild statutes from early modern dyeing towns list the plants a master may use and those he must avoid. Everything on the workshop shelves ______ if a visiting guild inspector found a single bolt colored with a banned dye. Historians read these harsh rules less as quality control than as protection for the dyers with access to the approved plants.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject is the indefinite pronoun "Everything," which is singular; "shelves," the plural noun just before the blank, sits inside the phrase "on the workshop shelves" and is not the subject. The verb must also be past, because the if-clause in the same sentence is in the past tense ("if a visiting guild inspector found a single bolt"), describing what happened whenever an inspection turned up a banned dye. Only "was forfeit" is both singular and past. "were forfeit" is past but plural, agreeing with "shelves." "is forfeit" is singular but present, which cannot be paired with the past "found," and "are forfeit" is both plural and present.
topic_tag: craft history: banned dyes in guild workshops

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement with a singular head noun followed by of + a gerund phrase whose object is plural, crossed with past progressive versus present perfect progressive decided by a past-tense verb in a before-clause of the same sentence
passage: Nineteenth-century etiquette manuals devote whole chapters to the calling card, a small printed card left at a house to announce a visit. The practice of exchanging such cards ______ slowly but steadily through provincial towns before the railway reached them, according to the order books of local printers. Social historians treat those order books as a rough map of middle-class ambition.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject is "practice," a singular noun; "cards," the plural noun just before the blank, is the object of the gerund "exchanging" inside the phrase "of exchanging such cards." The verb must also be past progressive rather than present perfect progressive, because the before-clause in the same sentence names a completed past event ("before the railway reached them"), and the present perfect cannot be anchored to a finished past moment. Only "was spreading" is singular and non-perfect. "were spreading" is past but plural, agreeing with "cards." "has been spreading" is singular but cannot take "before the railway reached them," and "have been spreading" is both plural and perfect.
topic_tag: social history: calling-card etiquette

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement in a main clause with a plural subject after an opening concessive clause whose subject is singular, crossed with simple past versus present perfect passive decided by a definite-past when-clause of the same sentence
passage: Although the household inventory lists each chair and candlestick in the house, the painted hall screens ______ without a single written note when a new owner emptied the west wing for use as a school. Decorative arts historians therefore rely on an auction catalog to trace them. Its descriptions are brief, but they match two screens that hang in a regional museum.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject of the main clause is "screens," a plural noun; "inventory," the singular subject of the opening "Although" clause, belongs to a different clause and cannot govern this verb. The verb must also be simple past rather than present perfect, because the when-clause in the same sentence fixes a finished past moment ("when a new owner emptied the west wing"), and the present perfect cannot take a definite past time. Only "were removed" is plural and simple past. "was removed" is simple past but singular, as if "inventory" were the subject. "have been removed" is plural but present perfect, which clashes with "emptied," and "has been removed" is both singular and perfect.
topic_tag: decorative arts history: a country-house inventory

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement with a plural head noun followed by an of-phrase ending on a singular noun, crossed with the number of the demonstrative pronoun that or those standing for the compared head
passage: Three illustrated copies of a town chronicle survive, and historians long disagreed about which of them served as the model for the others. A pigment analysis has offered an answer. The pigments of the smallest copy ______ of the two larger copies almost exactly, a match that points to a single workshop working over a short span of time.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject is "pigments," a plural noun; "copy," the singular noun just before the blank, is only the object of "of" in "of the smallest copy." The demonstrative stands for the thing being compared, which is the pigments of each copy, so it must also be plural: the sentence compares the pigments of one copy with the pigments ("those") of the other two. Only "match those" has both a plural verb and a plural demonstrative. "matches those" has the right demonstrative but a singular verb that agrees with "copy." "match that" has the right verb, but "that" would need a singular noun to stand for, and the only candidate, "copy," makes no sense ("the copy of the two larger copies"); "matches that" is wrong on both counts.
topic_tag: codicology: dating sister copies of a town chronicle

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement with a plural subject in the second clause of a compound sentence joined by so, crossed with the number of a possessive pronoun whose antecedent is the singular subject of the first clause
passage: A remote mountain shrine kept no written register of any kind, so the painted wooden tablets ______ only record of the pilgrimage. Each tablet shows a horse, a ship, or a sick child, and historians of religion have dated hundreds of them by their painting style and by the age of the wood. The oldest examples predate the shrine's main hall.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject of the second clause is "tablets," a plural noun, so the verb must be plural; "shrine," the singular subject of the first clause, belongs to that clause. The possessive, however, refers to the owner of the record, and the first clause names it: the shrine "kept no written register," so the tablets serve as the shrine's only record. Only "are its" pairs a plural verb with the singular possessive. "are their" has the right verb, but no plural noun in the sentence could own the record, because the tablets cannot be their own record. "is its" has the right possessive but a singular verb that agrees with "shrine" rather than "tablets," and "is their" is wrong on both counts.
topic_tag: religious history: votive tablets at a mountain shrine

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement in a direct question whose singular subject follows the auxiliary after plural nouns earlier in the sentence, crossed with do versus be as the auxiliary decided by the base verb after the subject
passage: Architectural historians who compare the cathedrals of two rival river towns keep returning to one question: why ______ taller and more elaborately carved west tower stop short of the spire drawn in its plans? Some blame a collapse in the wool trade that funded the work; others suspect that the foundations could not carry more weight.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: In this direct question the auxiliary comes before the subject, which is "tower" ("the taller and more elaborately carved west tower"), a singular noun; the plural nouns earlier in the sentence ("historians," "cathedrals," "towns") and the "and" joining two descriptive words do not make the subject plural. The auxiliary must also be a form of "do," because the verb that completes it, "stop," is a base form; a form of "be" would need "stopping." Only "does the" is singular and a form of "do." "do the" is a form of "do" but plural. "is the" is singular but cannot combine with "stop," and "are the" is both plural and the wrong auxiliary.
topic_tag: architectural history: an unfinished cathedral tower

subskill: boundaries: comma after an opening infinitive phrase of purpose whose final noun could be misread as the start of the main clause
passage: An oral history project recorded more than three hundred hours of conversation with retired dockworkers. To transcribe the ______ volunteers first split each tape into ten-minute segments. The speakers often used harbor slang that appears in no dictionary. Readers who knew the dockside dialect then checked each segment against the original sound.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The sentence opens with an introductory infinitive phrase of purpose, "To transcribe the interviews," and the main clause begins with its subject, "the volunteers." A comma after "interviews" marks where the introductory phrase ends. With no mark, "the interviews the volunteers first split" reads as a single noun phrase, and the sentence then breaks down at "each tape." A period after "interviews" leaves "To transcribe the interviews" as a fragment with no main clause, and a comma placed after "the" separates the article from the noun it introduces.
topic_tag: oral history: transcribing dockworkers' interviews

subskill: boundaries: no punctuation around a restrictive appositive name after a role noun when the passage names several holders of the role
passage: Three translators shared the work on the first English edition of a long nineteenth-century novel, dividing its chapters roughly into thirds. Reviewers were divided about the result, but they agreed in praising the chapters by the ______ for their ease and wit. Those chapters were later reprinted as a separate volume.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: Because the passage names three translators, "the translator" alone does not say which one is meant; the name "Ruiz" is essential to identify which translator wrote the praised chapters, so it is a restrictive appositive and takes no punctuation. Setting the name off with a pair of commas ("translator, Ruiz,") or a pair of dashes ("translator—Ruiz—") would mark it as extra information, wrongly implying that the edition had only one translator. "translator, Ruiz—" opens with a comma and closes with a dash, two marks that cannot work as a pair.
topic_tag: translation history: a jointly translated novel
